ancient_authors.name: Plutarch (Lives of Caesar & Mark Antony)
ancient_authors.genre: Moral Biography (Prescribed Set Text: Caesar 48–49; Antony 24–37, 51, 53–79, 81–86)
ancient_authors.strengths: Used eyewitness testimony from his own great-grandfather Nicarchus and Cleopatra’s physician Olympus; praises Cleopatra’s wit, nine languages, and golden Tarsus barge.
ancient_authors.limitations: Frames Antony’s career as a moral tragedy of a noble Roman general enslaved by Eastern luxury and passion.
ancient_authors.examiner_trap_warning: 2025 Examiner Report Warning: NEVER use TikTok slang ("gaslighter", "toxic", "simp") or call Caesarion "heir to the Roman throne" (Rome was a Republic that hated kings!).

ancient_authors.name: Horace, Virgil, Velleius, Suetonius, Dio & Contemporary Coinage
ancient_authors.time_gap: Contemporary Augustan poetry & coinage to imperial Roman history
ancient_authors.genre: Augustan Triumphal Poetry (Horace Odes 1.37; Virgil Aeneid 8.675–713) vs Ptolemaic/Antonian Coins
ancient_authors.strengths: Cleopatra’s own Egyptian bronze Isis coin (with baby Caesarion) and the 32 BC Antony/Cleopatra silver denarius show how she presented herself before Actium—directly countering hostile Roman stereotypes.
ancient_authors.limitations: Horace and Virgil wrote directly under Octavian/Augustus’ patronage to celebrate Actium as a civilizational war of Roman gods against monstrous Egyptian Anubis and a "fatale monstrum".
ancient_authors.examiner_trap_warning: On Q15* (20m), always contrast hostile Augustan literary set texts against Cleopatra’s contemporary coins and Dendera/Egyptian ideology!

key_individuals.name: Queen Cleopatra VII Philopator
key_individuals.role: Last Ptolemaic Pharaoh of Egypt (r. 51–30 BC)
achievements: First Ptolemaic monarch in 250 years to learn the Egyptian language alongside eight other tongues; revered by Egyptians as the living goddess Isis.
Secured Egypt’s independence and grain prosperity through strategic alliances with Julius Caesar (bearing Ptolemy XV Caesarion, 47 BC) and Mark Antony (recovering Cyprus, Cilicia, and Coele-Syria).
Commanded sixty Egyptian warships at Actium (31 BC) and chose royal suicide in Alexandria (August 30 BC) rather than march in chains in Octavian’s Roman triumph.
key_individuals.significance: Maintained Ptolemaic Egypt as the last independent Hellenistic kingdom in the Mediterranean for two decades against Roman annexation.
key_individuals.exam_distinction: Separate Cleopatra’s pragmatic Eastern dynastic statecraft from Octavian’s Roman senate propaganda.
